title: Label Vs Selector
body:
What is a label in Kubernetes?
Answer: A label is a key-value pair attached to a Kubernetes object such as a Pod, Deployment, or Service.
Example:
labels:
  app: web
Here:
Key = app
Value = web

What is a label selector?
A selector, on the other hand, is used to find or filter resources based on their labels. For example, -l app=web is a selector that tells Kubernetes to find Pods whose label is app=web. In simple terms, a label is like a tag attached to an object, while a selector is like a filter used to find objects having that tag. So, app=web on a Pod is the label, while -l app=web in kubectl get pods -l app=web is the selector.


Which Kubernetes resources can have labels?
Answer:
Almost every Kubernetes resource can have labels, including:
Pods
Deployments
Services
ReplicaSets
StatefulSets
DaemonSets
Nodes
Namespaces
Jobs
ConfigMaps
Secrets

What happens when you use -l app=web?
Answer: Kubernetes filters the Pods and returns only Pods having app=web.
For example:
Pod 1 → app=web       ✅
Pod 2 → app=api       ❌
Pod 3 → app=web       ✅
Result:
Pod 1
Pod 3


Can a Pod have multiple labels?
Answer: Yes.
Example:
labels:
  app: web
  environment: production
  version: v2
The Pod has three labels:
app=web
environment=production
version=v2


Can we select using multiple labels?
Answer: Yes.
Example:
kubectl get pods -n drill -l app=web,environment=production
This means:
Find Pods where app=web AND environment=production.

title: GKE Q&A
body:
what's the smallest unit in Kubernetes?":
"The container is the smallest unit of execution, but the Pod is the smallest unit Kubernetes schedules and manages. You never scale, restart, or schedule a container on its own — only a Pod."

Node "Standard vs Autopilot — when would you pick each?
Standard = you manage nodes, Google manages the control plane.
Autopilot = Google manages nodes and control plane; you only manage workloads (pods).

what's the relationship between gcloud and kubectl?":
"gcloud manages the cluster as infrastructure — creating, resizing, upgrading, deleting it. kubectl manages workloads running inside an existing cluster. get-credentials is the bridge: it authenticates kubectl to talk to a cluster gcloud already provisioned, but it doesn't give kubectl any of gcloud's infrastructure-level abilities."

"how does kubectl connect to GKE?":
"kubectl itself is cloud-agnostic — it just talks to whatever Kubernetes API server is listed as the current context in ~/.kube/config. gcloud container clusters get-credentials is the GCP-specific step that populates that file with GKE's API server address and wires up an auth plugin that fetches fresh tokens from your gcloud identity. From there, every request is gated by GCP IAM first, then Kubernetes RBAC."

why multiple node pools?":
"To match hardware to workload — different machine types, sizes, or pricing models (spot vs on-demand) — and scale each independently, with taints/node-selectors controlling which pods are allowed to schedule onto which pool."

note
One cluster → contains multiple node pools → each pool is a group of identical nodes (same machine type/size) → each pool's node count can be scaled independently of the others.
A cluster doesn't have to have all its nodes be the same size or type. Instead, GKE lets you group nodes into pools — and every node inside one pool is identical (same machine type, same disk size, same settings). If you want two different kinds of machines (say, cheap small ones for regular apps and expensive GPU ones for ML), you create two separate pools, each with its own name.
